title: Local-complete-intersection and pure-one-dimensional finite stages of a nodal limit
statement: Let $I$ be a nonempty directed set and $(S_i)_{i\in I}$ an inverse system of quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions] with affine transition morphisms [pqf-def-affine-morphism] and limit $S$ [lem-weil-pbc-limit-affine-transition]. Fix $a\in I$ and a finitely presented morphism $g_a:X_a\to S_a$ with $X_a$ quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Put $X_i=X_a\times_{S_a}S_i$, $g_i:X_i\to S_i$ for $i\ge a$, and $h:X=X_a\times_{S_a}S\to S$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. Here finitely presented means locally of finite presentation [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation], quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Assume $h$ is flat [def-weil-flat-morphism]. For every algebraically closed field $\Omega$ and geometric point $y:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S$ [def-weil-geometric-point], assume its geometric fibre $X_y$ [def-weil-geometric-fibre] is empty or pure of dimension $1$ [def-weil-pure-dimension], and at every point where $X_y\to\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ is not smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], its completed local ring [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion] is isomorphic to $\Omega[[u,v]]/(uv)$ [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Then there exists $c\ge a$ such that for every $i\ge c$, $g_i$ is flat and locally of finite presentation; every nonempty ordinary fibre [def-pc-scheme-fibre] of $g_i$ is pure of dimension $1$; and for every algebraically closed $\Omega$ and geometric point $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S_i$, the geometric fibre is empty or both pure of dimension $1$ and a local complete intersection over $\Omega$. A scheme locally of finite type over a field $k$ is a local complete intersection over $k$ if it admits an affine open cover by spectra of finitely generated $k$-algebras which are local complete intersections as defined in [def-weil-pbc-complete-intersection-over-field]; the empty scheme is allowed.

proof.text: Every base change of $g_a$, in particular $h$, is locally of finite presentation. Indeed on a finite-presentation affine chart $B=A[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$, scalar extension to an affine base chart $A\to A\prime$ gives $A\prime[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/(f_1\prime,\ldots,f_m\prime)$; these pulled-back charts cover the base change. The cited finite-presentation base-change result justifies this presentation. Such a presentation is also finitely generated, so all the morphisms and their field fibres in what follows are locally of finite type.

source.place: Tag 01TP (definition-finite-presentation); affine base-change calculation, algebra.tex Tag 05G5

proof.text: Fix a geometric point $y:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S$. If $X_y$ is empty, its empty affine cover gives the local-complete-intersection condition. Otherwise it is locally of finite type over $\Omega$ by Step 1 and pure of dimension $1$ by hypothesis. Every closed point is smooth or has the stated nodal completion. Apply the forward implication of the nodal-curve lci criterion with $k=\Omega$: since $\Omega$ is already algebraically closed, take its algebraic closure to be itself, so the completed geometric local ring in that criterion is exactly the one in the hypothesis. It follows that $X_y$ is a local complete intersection over $\Omega$. The additional unramified-singular-subscheme conclusion of the criterion is not needed.

Apply complete-intersection-fibres limit descent with $i_0=a$, $U_0=X_a$, $V_0=S_a$ and $g_0=g_a$, where $V_0$ has its identity $S_a$-structure. Its base changes are exactly $g_i$ and $h$. The required qcqs hypotheses are those on $X_a,S_a$; the affine transition and limit hypotheses are given; $g_a$ is locally finitely presented by hypothesis; $h$ is flat by hypothesis; and Step 2 supplies every geometric lci fibre. Thus there is $b\ge a$ such that for every $i\ge b$, $g_i$ is flat and locally finitely presented and every geometric fibre is a local complete intersection.

source.place: Tag 0C3L (lemma-descend-syntomic), as used in curves.tex Tag 0C5F first proof paragraph

proof.text: For each $s\in S$ put $k=\kappa(s)$ and $F=X_s$, and choose an algebraic closure $\bar k$ of $k$. The associated geometric point has fibre $F_{\bar k}$. The field-extension spectrum map is surjective and remains so after base change; hence $p:F_{\bar k}\to F$ is surjective. If $F$ is nonempty, so is $F_{\bar k}$, which is pure of dimension $1$ by hypothesis. The equidimensional-open local-dimension lemma with the whole open $F_{\bar k}$ gives $\dim_z F_{\bar k}=1$ at every point $z$. Given $x\in F$, choose $z$ above it; the field-extension local-dimension formula gives $\dim_x F=\dim_z F_{\bar k}=1$. The same field-extension lemma applied to the identity extension $k/k$ shows that $F$ is locally Noetherian. The constant-local-dimension component lemma, with the whole open $F$, now shows every component of $F$ has dimension $1$. Thus every nonempty ordinary fibre of $h$ is pure of dimension $1$. Empty fibres cause no restriction.

source.place: Tag 02FY (lemma-dimension-fibre-after-base-change), part (1); varieties.tex Tag 0A21 (lemma-dimension-locally-algebraic), parts (3),(5); morphisms.tex Tag 01S1

proof.text: Apply pure-relative-dimension finite-stage descent with $i_0=a$, $Y_0=X_a$, $Z_0=S_a$, $f_0=g_a$ and $d=1$. These are qcqs schemes over $S_a$, the initial morphism is locally of finite presentation, and Step 4 is exactly its pure ordinary-fibre hypothesis at the limit. Obtain $d_0\ge a$ such that every nonempty ordinary fibre of every $g_i$ for $i\ge d_0$ is pure of dimension $1$.

Choose a common upper bound $c$ of $b$ and $d_0$. For $i\ge c$ Step 3 supplies flatness, local finite presentation and geometric lci fibres, while Step 5 supplies pure-one-dimensional ordinary fibres. Apply relative-dimension base change to $g_i$ and any geometric point $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S_i$. Its base change has base a field, whose unique ordinary fibre is the geometric fibre in question. Consequently each nonempty such fibre is pure of dimension $1$, and it is lci by Step 3. These are all the required conclusions, simultaneously for every $i\ge c$.
